utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We start today with French. I think it's been resolved. Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just before we adjourned yesterday, I had asked you about something you said during the course of the Stanisic/Zupljanin case with reference to what you called the vain professor types, and your reference to the fact that it seemed important for them "to have photographs taken with them," that is, photographs with paramilitary figures and those professor types you're referring to, and you confirmed that. That was at page 4649 yesterday. I wanted then to show you an image and ask you whether or not that was one of the types of photo opportunities or photos that you were referring to. And if we could play 40146 in Sanction for the benefit of the witness and the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a very brief clip, Mr. Mandic. We can play it again, but you may have already recognised the persons depicted in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it be -- could it be played again? My screen was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you -- first of all, do you recognise the persons shown in that brief video-clip?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this happened before the war in Bijeljina, when there were inter-ethnic tensions mounting, and Biljana Plavsic, as a member of the Presidency, and Fikret Abdic, with some members of the government, went to Bijeljina on that occasion because of that, and I believe -- and this was something which was repeatedly aired on BH Television, that she is here hugging and kissing with Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan. I believe this took place in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. And was that one of the images you had in mind when you referred to having photographs taken with paramilitary figures?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rather believe that this person that I spoke about a bit emotionally yesterday did a job that she wasn't really good at doing, and then, in a sort of exhibitionist way, sought to acquire popularity among the people and become a leader of the people in the given circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 40146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1108.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, yesterday there was reference to the 22nd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in Zvornik in November of 1992. That document was admitted. You referred to comments made by a number of individuals, including Mrs. Plavsic, at that session, and I wanted to look briefly at comments by Mrs. Plavsic at page 20 of the English and the bottom of page 19 and page 20 of the B/C/S. And I believe that's now P1105. And, of course, we'll have to leave Sanction and get back into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for housekeeping purposes, before we address this excerpt, I need to note that the time or code for the previous exhibit was 01:48:20 to 01:48:33. That's the portion that was played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, as indicated, Mr. Mandic, the portion of P1105 now shown on the screen reflects remarks by Ms. Plavsic on that date, who says: "I first want to say something that refers to me personally, since Mico Stanisic mentioned my name. I want to avoid any misunderstandings, because people say many things, mostly about the crime that's destroying our country and our people. I don't want you to think this is some kind of rumour. I'd like to respond to Minister Stanisic. It is the truth, not rumour, Minister, that after the statement by the president of the republic, i.e., his call to volunteers in all Serbian lands and all other Orthodox countries, I sent letters to all addresses. My intention was to pay anybody who is willing to fight for the Serbian cause and gather them around, so letters went out. You talk about paramilitary and non-paramilitary formations. You will have to excuse me. That has nothing to do with me. I was looking for the people who are willing to fight for the Serbian cause, who are willing to fight in the territory of Republika Srpska. The letters were sent to the Soviet Union, to Seselj, Arkan and Jovanovic. Do as you like. Accuse me now if you want. I want to make it clear, because this is the second time, Minister, it's not hearsay, I did do it, and you can judge me if you want." And "Applause" is indicated in the transcript. Mr. Mandic, is this the -- are these the comments by Mrs. Plavsic that you were referring to yesterday, at least in part, when discussing her invitations to paramilitaries to come to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, were you aware that -- aware of whether other Bosnian Serb leaders thought highly of Arkan and wanted to have him come to Republika Srpska or, indeed, wanted to have their pictures taken with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me show you next, then, 65 ter 4508, another video-clip for which we'll have to move to Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is a video-clip from October 23, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Sir, the Battalion of the Serbian Volunteer Guard is lined up in your honour, sir. Ranks ready for inspection." "For the Guard, and for you as the commander of the Guard." "Thank you very much, Mr. President. Gratitude for you being here. This is not the end, it is the beginning. Thank you very much. Mr. President, would you be so kind as to say a few words?" "I'm deeply thankful and I congratulate you, and I hope that we will meet again in peace, and you always will have a place in the heart of those whom you have defended. Thank you." "Mr. President, in the name of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, I wish to say two words to you, which is we are ready if you call us, and that we will be back to defend our eternal homeland, to defend our women and children, to defend Serbian territory and our Orthodox religion. Thank you, Mr. President." "Cheers." "Very well, Mr. President. We are going back now. I want to thank you once again." "Goodbye." "Here we are. We will come, and we will stay in contact."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, first of all, although I think I know the answer to that, were you aware of this particular ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. This is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does that refresh your recollection about the extent of the support for Arkan or other paramilitaries by members of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you try to identify the persons in the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I should have done that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just for the benefit of the record and the Court, can you indicate whether you recognised any of the persons depicted in the video?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the video, I recognised the president of the Serbian Republic, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, and Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, the commander of the Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. And I had asked, before we completed that, whether reviewing or seeing this video refreshed your recollection about the extent of the support for Arkan or other paramilitaries by members of the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we have seen from all this so far, Biljana Plavsic was in charge of the inviting of such paramilitary units and of contacts with them. She was the bridge between the Bosnian Serbs, who were waging war in Bosnia, and these people, who came from other states, to the best of my knowledge, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 40548.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't believe this witness has been able to speak to this. This occurred after he left. He said he was not familiar with the ceremony. All he's done is identified two of the people who are in this, and I don't think this is a proper witness to lay the foundation for this exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But is the content not related to the subject-matter of his testimony, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but I don't believe that makes it admissible. And it's broadly related, but it's not -- he's not able to provide any foundation for the -- for the accuracy of what's depicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, Mr. Tieger, there's no link that connects the video to the witness, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would note that -- I'm sorry that I didn't have an opportunity to speak before the Chamber conferred, but I would note the following with respect to the nexus or the link: The issue raised was invitations to the paramilitary, and interactions with the paramilitary, support of the paramilitary, et cetera. The focus was on Mrs. Plavsic, who was a member of the Presidency with Dr. Karadzic and a close associate with Dr. Karadzic. The excerpt from the 22nd Session, which we read, said: "After the statement of the president of the republic," that's Dr. Karadzic, "i.e. his call to volunteers in all Serbian lands and all other countries, Mrs. Plavsic reacted." It was testimony in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case which we heard concerning Mr. Mandic's reaction to Dr. Karadzic's support for Mrs. Plavsic. This is a document that would come in, in my submission, in every stringent common-law jurisdiction. There's no question about the accuracy of this document. It's a videotape, and I don't think Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic are going to contest that this videotape accurately depicts what's shown in the video. And it's Dr. Karadzic who is depicted on that video. It is a wholly appropriate moment for the admission of this document, certainly more appropriate for a subsequent submission -- or at least as appropriate as a subsequent submission linked to the bulk of the evidence through written submissions in the form of a Bar table or having a witness come in and say, These are videotapes of the accused's link with paramilitary figures. And I would ask the Court to reconsider, in light of that -- and I say again I'm quite sure that this is the case that this is the kind of document that Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic want to see come in in this fashion. They're simply noting their objection to previous rulings in response to their submissions and, I think, trying to find parallels there. Now, as I say, I think there are clear distinguishing factors, but I believe if pressed, Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic would say this is an appropriate point at which to submit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic, would you like to have a say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to say this: This is a question of principle, but not only of principle, but of the essence. Biljana Plavsic and what the witness spoke about referred to 1992. This is 1995. Apart from that, in various instances we offered documents which refer to that phenomenon, and nothing was admitted. Let us have another witness for that. This is not detrimental to the Defence at all, but it is a question of principle. This is out of context. We asked for some documents to be admitted in context which directly refer to the subject-matter at hand, whereas this is totally out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, there's no issue as to the relevancy or the accuracy of the video-clip, and I agree that that may be a subject of a separate Bar table motion in the later stage. What concerns is the proper control of the conduct of the examination. In order to put something to the witness, there should be some nexus or links. Otherwise, in a trial of this size, there will be no end, in particular, in the face of cross-examination. That's the perspective of the Chamber as at this moment, and I think the Chamber has tried, on several occasions, to make the position of the Chamber understood to the parties. So this will not be admitted, as we indicated, and let's move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, yesterday we presented a number of documents reflecting a contemporaneous awareness of Arkan's presence in Sarajevo. Were you aware that Arkan was working with or in communication with Bosnian Serb political or military authorities in the spring or summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Biljana Plavsic communicated with Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, from March 1992. As for others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me ask you a background question. Who was Radmila?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me play, then, for you 65 ter 30666. And, Your Honour, although the previous video-clip was not admitted, perhaps it's useful, nevertheless, to indicate the time code of that exhibit that was played today, and that would be 00:01:00 to 00:04:05.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Good day. Staff of Serbian Volunteer Guard." "Good day." "I'm calling you from the Serb MUP in Sarajevo." "From the Serb?" "Sarajevo SUP, Secretariat of the Interior." "Yes?" "Tell me, which of our men, and what is the number of Zvornik police station? Who do we have in Zvornik?" "Just a minute." "And who is in control of Zvornik?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I wanted to indicate to you this is an intercepted telephone conversation of the 16th of April, 1992. And if we could proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello." "Hello." "Good day." "Serb MUP." "Yes." "Sarajevo." "Who is in control of Zvornik, and do we have a police station in Zvornik?" "And where are you calling from?" "From Sarajevo." "Just a second, just a minute." "Thanks a lot. Hello." "Yes." "Who is this?" "Radmila. Who is there?" "Arkan speaking." "Arkan, this is Radmila." "Now I will tell you which one." "Aha. " "The one Zoran Kalezic told you about, but you cannot remember, and through Buda Markovic." "Oh, yes, yes." "Listen, man, one of our men fell in Zvornik. He was returning from Belgrade. He pulled out a family ..." "What did he do?" "Well, he fell, he was caught in Zvornik." "How in heaven's name in Zvornik?" "Well, that's exactly what we're asking ourselves." "But I don't understand. How come he fell in Zvornik?" "Here's what happened. He was working for us ... he was working under Momo Mandic." "Yes." "... yesterday, he drove the family of Momo's brother, Mladjen, to Belgrade." "Yes." "... and he was on his way back. Mladjo, what's the name of the man -- no, the man in Zvornik who caught him? Arkan, some Sabic." "Who the fuck is Sabic?" "I don't know. Look now, the kid used to drive for Hilmo in the brewery, he used to work for him, and now we do not know what to do. Hilmo, I guess that Sabic had called Hilmo to let him know. Hilmo said: 'The kid went to look for nitrogen, let him go,' ammoniac, ammoniac, under the pretence it was for the brewery, you know? However, they are not willing to let him go because the car is ours, the SUP's, the car in which they caught him, a Golf, with registration plates." "They caught him in Zvornik?" "He says he fell in Zvornik: "Well, it is impossible in Zvornik, Zvo..." "My opinion in Zvornik. " "There is nobody, it is certainly not Zvornik." "Where could he fall?" "I do not know, but it is not in Zvornik. The Serbs are in control of Zvornik." "Well, he called and said he was in Zvornik." "He called?" "That Sabic called and said that he was caught in Zvornik." "In Zvornik, no way. Surely not in Zvornik." "Well, tell me, please, on his way to Belgrade, via Zvornik to Sarajevo, is there a village or a backwater town, is there anybody, anything where they are holding, where the road for us is not safe?" "To tell you the truth, I do not know. I do not have a clue." "You do not know?" "I do not know." "We do not know. You know what, at this point in time we still cannot show our cards to them, so they would not realise that they caught a big-shot, you know?" "Yes, yes." "Well, I mean, he's not a big-shot, but he is working for us, yes." "Well, I mean, I don't know, I do not know at all." "And do you have your men in Zvornik who might have some knowledge on where he might be?" "Well, no. I pulled my men out of Zvornik." "Oh, you pulled your men out of Zvornik?" "Well, of course, you can see they are after me. Do you not know what the situation is?" "I know everything, man, there's everything ... they are after us, as well, it seems like the whole world is after us." "I pulled out my men because ..." "The Serbs down there in Zvornik to control." "The Serbs and the army are down there." "Do you know any -- well, it's of no use even if we know now." "I will now call the Crisis Staff down there to see what is happening." "Give it to us, too, we also do not have it down here." "Where are the numbers of the Crisis Staff in Zvornik? Give it to me." "What is the name of the kid?" "Dejan." "Dejan." "Dejan Markovic, Dejan Markovic, come on." "Here you go." "705." "All right." "584." "All right." "704." "704. Any other?" "And 075." "All right." "584-685." "685." "I will call them immediately." "Please do so. When will you be coming here?" "Sorry?" "When will you be coming here?" "Ha, eh, eh." "How are your children?" "Fine." "All right. Well, come visit us as well." "Well I do not know what all of you want me." "What do you think? Why is that?" "But you should realise the situation, which is ..." "Well, we do, we realise it, but in vain." "Ah?" "In vain, Arkan, in vain. In vain, I don't know, well it is not in vain, look ..." "Wait, where are you now?" "I am in our staff, up there in Vrace, in the school." "Aha." "This is the only thing we are holding in Sarajevo. Do you have our number?" "I have all of the numbers. I talked to that guy Stanisic, and ..." "Yes, Mico Stanisic, rush him away from Pale. What are they doing up there?" "Fuck them, how should I know what they're doing?" "Why don't they come down from Pale to the city instead of ..." "I have another line, I will talk to them, and you stay on the line." "All right. Go ahead, Arkan." "So, you are in Sarajevo?" "We are in Sarajevo, in that school in Vrace." "Well, are you holding at least that ... ?" "We are holding that. Look, we are holding ... Arkan, we could hold everything, if only someone gave us the order to go. I don't know what they're waiting for." "Well, that's it." "Well, why wait? Because America is threatening Serbia; right?" "That's it." "And we are scared." "That is the thing, they are all chickens." "Chicken, of course. And they let the time go." "That is what we ..." "We lost the time, we should have -- we should have when ..." "Nobody is answering this phone, 584-704." "That is -- no way. You should not have allowed them that, they start slacking." "Hey, wait, wait. I will know. I have this other number ..." "Do that. Nobody is answering the Zvornik Crisis Staff today." "That is it." "Did you hear from Buda?" "No." "Why?" "Well, it's been a long time since we talked. Tell me one thing, please. Well ..." "Go ahead." "So Sarajevo, you control at least one part of it?" "We control one part, and they do not dare even show their heads in that part. We could control a large part of Sarajevo. Look now, we could push them into their own part of town. But why does not -- why doesn't anyone give us that order?" "Well, Karadzic should do that. Do you have his phone number?" "Up there in Pale?" "Well, yes, of course I do, when they are coming and going and they leave." "Why don't you ask him, he is kind of an official representative now?" "We have just received information they are drawing the map and they are in Pale." "What?" "They are in Pale, only Momo, deputy minister is here." "Yes, yes. And what can he do? He can do nothing." "Well, he cannot do a thing until they have issued an order. The army is here, everything is here, but it's in vain." "Well, the army also escaped. They were threatened with planes, and they ran away." "Where?" "Ah?" "Where are they are, here?" "Well, the army threatened them, I mean the Americans threatened them." "The Americans?" "Well, yes." "That inform -- well, all right, these people certainly know that." "Fuck them all." "Well, they should send it. Why did they not send it to Croatia, to Zagreb?" "Who?" "Well, America." "There is no choice. You can see that the world public is accusing us of being the aggressor." "Yes, I would not really be scared." "Well, we are not afraid. We can only die once, not 100 times." "Only once, yes ... I would not pay much ..." "None of us gives a fuck, to be honest." "Right, I would not." "That is why we have to be careful. You see that 17.000 children came here from Sarajevo." "And now what happens, we wait; right? And let them have it." "Yesterday some kid, an ambassador was here ..." "Well, to hell with her." "She says she is the ambassador of children, she drove ..." "She is the ambassador of Alija's children." "No, no, ours, our children." "Ah, our children?" "Yes, ours. Her name is Vidakovic." "Vidakovic." "Yes. Her mother and father are in France." "That is all theirs, that is all a part of their politics. I do not believe a thing. Credit to them for working for children, but ..." "They moved us out. Fuck them." "Yes." "Excuse me for expressing myself this way, but that is how things are." "You just ..." "This other number is busy all the time." "685; right?" "Yes, yes, and there it is ringing, but nobody is answering. We will try again. Listen." "Go ahead." "Come on, call in some time, or ... you understand." "This same number?" "Yes." "Okay, I will call you again." "Cheers." "Cheers."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Mandic, did you recognise any of the voices involved in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not recognise a single voice. I don't have any of these voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The intercept indicates it's a conversation between Radmila Kalaba and Zeljko Raznatovic, aka Arkan. I asked you before if you knew who Radmila was. Can you tell us anything about Radmila, a Radmila who was connected with the Serbian MUP in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Radmila Kalaba is. She's probably some administrator, a person working in the Serb police. I don't know. I cannot remember that name, the first or the last name. It's one of the desk officers there, probably. Now, whether that person worked in the police then or before that, I'm just sure that before the war that person did not work for the police, and I don't know the name of Radmila Kalaba at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's set aside the last name for a moment. Did you know the name of a woman named Radmila who worked for you and was involved on at least more than one occasion in calling persons on your behalf to make contact with them on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My secretary was Radmila Radojcic before the war in the joint MUP, and for a while she was with me in Vraca in the Ministry of Justice. However, this is not that person. This was Radmila Radojcic. Obviously, it's not this same person, Radmila Kalaba. It was a completely different person who worked with me or was my secretary, rather, Radmila Radojcic. I think that right now she works in the police centre in Bijeljina. Before the war and during the war, she worked for the Ministry of Justice, and she was my secretary. This Kalaba, I don't know who she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we see from this conversation, this Radmila is calling in connection with a person who was thought to have been -- to have fallen or been taken captive in Zvornik, someone who was working under Momo Mandic, she says, and who drove the family of Momo's brother, Mladen, to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm aware of this particular event. I first listened to this conversation during the proofing with Ms. Korner, the Prosecutor here. I first heard it two or three months ago. This Dejan Markovic was a driver in the brewery. Hilmo Selimovic was the director, and he was assistant minister in the joint Ministry of the Police. He was my friend, a local Sarajevo man. This young man, who was about 20 at the time, drove my brother's family to Belgrade. My brother was also a policeman. He was a teacher at the Police School. He was arrested at some point by an armed Muslim group, and this Kalaba probably knew what telephone -- knew various telephone numbers and had contact with Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan. Hilmo Selimovic helped me a great deal, at my insistence, and he found this young man somewhere, I don't know, in some town, and there was this exchange. And I know that this young man was saved thanks to Hilmo Selimovic and his acquaintances who had arrested this young man who was about 20 at the time. As for this conversation, I first heard it when I was being proofed by Ms. Korner, and this Radmila certainly did not work for the police before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether she advised you of the information she had gathered, in connection with that incident, from Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I don't know who Radmila is, Radmila Kalaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the circumstances in Zvornik, as related in this intercept, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know what I know from this conversation. I did not know what was happening in Zvornik. Well, you see from the conversation, itself, that this woman does not know who is in Zvornik and what is going on there, and that she is not aware of the facts involved. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to tender this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would object to it, first of all, on relevance grounds. I'm not sure, really, how it relates to the case against Dr. Karadzic. Secondly, to the extent that the witness has been able to speak to the document, it's only about a tangential issue concerning his brother's transportation and not about anything that is really relevant to the case, so I don't believe it's admissible. If for any reason you did think it was admissible, I think it would only be able to be marked for identification at this point, since it's not a conversation that the witness can authenticate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to reply, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if the Court requires me to reply with reference to the relevance. This -- I hardly know where to start. This is contact by the Serbian MUP, according to the intercept, to determine what's happening in Zvornik. Arkan has -- relates his relationship with the Serbian authorities in Zvornik and leaving matters in their hands. There's a question of when he might come. The connection between -- the linkage between Dr. Karadzic and the Serbian MUP has been made clear on a number of occasions, in a number of ways. I just tried to tender a document related to Dr. Karadzic's interaction with Arkan, himself. I could go on and on, but I don't think that's the issue. As far as MFI'ing it, I appreciate the fact that this witness has not identified the participants in the intercept, but has, instead, talked to some extent about some of what's related in the content of that discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Although the witness was not able to identify the voices in the intercept, the witness's name was referred to in this intercept and the witness confirmed the event referred to in the intercept. So, as such, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P1109, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, on Thursday, I believe it was, you asked -- you referred to an intercept in your intercept binder, involving you and Mr. Prstojevic, and asked if that could be played. In fact, you asked twice to hear that intercept. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, when I asked him to return this judge, a Muslim, to his job, because he had dismissed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Mandic, you indicated, when you were referring to this intercept, that it was about the complete blockade of the municipality and about Judge Musanovic, but, in fact, the discussion was broader than that. It was about ethnic cleansing of Ilidza; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Could I have this other part? Or, actually, could I have a look at the binder, and then I can look it up in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You can do both. We'll play the intercept, and you can have the binder with you at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's play the intercept, then, if possible, but the entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's at tab 17 of your binder, Mr. Mandic. Your Honours, that's 65 ter 30829. And, again, we have to move to Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we start again? Is Sanction on?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Good afternoon." "Good afternoon." "Serb Ministry of Justice. May I get through to Mr. Prstojevic through this number, please?" "Who wants to speak to him?" "The minister." "The minister?" "Momcilo Mandic, the minister of justice." "Aha, Momcilo Mandic, one moment, please." "Thank you." "Hello." "Yes." "Mr. Prstojevic?" "Speaking." "One moment, please." "Hello." "Hello." "Good afternoon." "Good fortune to you, Prstojevic." "How are you?" "Very well, and how are you?" "Very well. Who am I talking to?" "It's Momo Mandic." "Momo Mandic, the Minister of Justice." "Yes, that's right. That's right." "No minister has a more beautiful name?" "That's right." "Because there is nothing more beautiful than justice, is there?" "That's right. We just need to achieve it." "A ..." "Listen, Prstojevic, listen to me, do you have any problems in Ilidza? Is anyone bothering you? Are they attacking you?" "No, no one is bothering me." "You're not letting them, are you?" "That's right. Whoever bothers me, I get hold of a weapon and start shooting. When the Turks bother me and my army, I get hold of weapons and defend ..." "Are you from Herzegovina or Zagora?" "Well, not really. I'm an Orthodox Herzegovinian." "A Herzegovinian, is it?" "Well, Kalinovik is my municipality." "Aha. I have two questions for you." "Yes." "It has come to our attention and that of the government that you are issuing ultimatums to some Turks; evicting people from certain settlements and people respond badly to it. They are abusing this, those Muslims and the media and so on." "Yes." "Well, please do not do anything like it. Consult with Djeric first and those people up there, because this is very bad publicity for us and for everyone. You have to be more flexible there and not touch those Muslims who are willing to listen, who are loyal. We cannot ethnically cleanse Ilidza or any other place. At least that is the attitude of the government and political leadership and all. It has already reached the top how in some settlement you gave them 24 hours to move out and they ... well, no, not the safety ... what was it? What did you say? You are not ... you are not responsible for their safety or something like that." "Well, yes, but where did I say this?" "Well, people you have to ..." "I know, but we did not say that, not in public. That is not our policy." "I know, I know what it should be and how we should operate and so ..." "Yes, but we do not say that in public, nor do we write it." "Please, in that context, you know what is necessary. You were probably up there during the talks and that and how it should be done, and those Muslims who said that about us, we have to ... it's some sort of protection, mother-fuckers, as long as they listen, behave. In that context, Fadil Musanovic is a judge. But, look, talk to him. If he has not already fled, place him to work for us, so that we can say that we employ everyone, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, regardless of ethnicity, as long as they are loyal to the Serb state. So have a look, please. Place two or three Muslims somewhere, mother-fuckers, let ..." "You know what, Momo?" "What?" "Even with the best of intentions, with all the Muslims from Ilidza have already done, and what they are doing, let's say, as long as there is a blockade of the Serbs in Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija, it's been a month since no Serb has come out." "I know. My sister and my father are there." "No one has come out of there, despite the fact that we allow it. Let them come out now. Let them have 5.000 Muslims from there. Let them release as many Serbs. We are not in a position to let someone work at the moment. Our Misdemeanor Court did not receive a single report. No one submitted any." "Well, push Tomo Kovac and the police. Make them work. They are looting there, they're disrupting public peace and order. You are the government there, so force these people to work. Make them arrest people. Lots of things are going on. I don't mean in Ilidza, specifically, but across this republic of ours. There are gangs, thieves, war profiteers, so let the police do their job. Force them, hold a meeting with them. If the Court is operational, it is supposed to work. Let there believe report, let them work." "Yes." "Look, I think it would be good politically. I don't want to insist on it. It's not up to me. Ilidza is not mine. It was not, everything, in the media and this and that, just like they take Pejanovic or Kecmanovic or anyone of ours and then the entire world knows about it. I think that we have to learn certain things even from these Muslims." "Yes." "For the general public and all, I mean, if there is not somewhere, there are others, and other work positions, and to say, to publish that, put it on television, 'Srna,' and then Belgrade and so on, not only Ilidza but other areas also look into that." "Tell me, tell me, when are you ..." "I'm in Kula all the time, or rather in Lukavica." "All right, I'll stop by as soon as I have the chance ..." "Please do come ..." "... to talk over coffee and ..." "Well, yes, okay, then, agreed." " ... the Serb municipality of Ilidza, you see. Because I see that they have some, let's say, even territorial differences, they are appear in the organisation of judicial system and so on." "All right, no problems. That is normal, we will sit down and discuss. There are no problems, whenever you come, stop by and we will agree." "I will stop by." "Agreed. But, please, have a look with your associates, with Tomo Kovac, to work on that, for people to be punished, because these criminals and profiteers are extremely active." "That's right, but you see, only the other day we received ..." "All right, all right, now you need to get involved and press Kovac to work." "Yes, 'Official Gazette' number 6. We only received it the day before yesterday." "Yes, yes." "Only now we have the legal basis we can start with work." "Excellent, excellent. Go on. Let that be adopted for people to see that Serbs do not ... that they do not drink and that they are not firing cannon, but that we work, that we are normal people and that we want a legal state protecting all of our inhabitants and all the rest." "All right, Momo." "Talk to you later." "All right, then." "Cheers."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Mandic, do you recognise the participants in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is I and Prstojevic, Nedjeljko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You asked to have that played. Does hearing it now refresh your recollection that it concerned information you had that Prstojevic had commenced or was engaged in ethnic cleansing in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reached the prime minister, Mr. Djeric, up there at the government, and he informed me about this. And, of course, he said that I should carefully talk to Mr. Prstojevic, and that he should not block normal life in Ilidza, and that he should not dismiss people just because they're Muslims. Mr. Tieger, for example, Prstojevic is saying that specifically here, in Hrasnica there were a certain number of Serbs who had lived there, and they were detained in the school or the health centre in Hrasnica. Now, both of them were trying to see how they -- since they could keep detained Serbs in Hrasnica, then we could do the same thing in Ilidza. I was trying to explain that to him, that that was wrong, and the Serb state could not be created that way, and that people should not be blocked or detained in that way, or dismissed from their jobs, just because they're of a different ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, you seem to be focusing on blocking or dismissing, but you direct Mr. Prstojevic's attention in this intercept to evicting people. And, in fact, that was the information you had from Tomo Kovac, among others; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, no, I didn't have it. I had information from Mr. Djeric that Prstojevic had told the Muslims in a part of the Ilidza settlement that he would not guarantee -- could not guarantee their security there if they remained, which was very bad both for the Serbian Republic, and for the politics pursued by the Serbian people, and for everybody. And we tried to persuade Prstojevic not to do that, that he could not seek to conduct ethnic cleansing in such a way or to intimidate others, non-Serbs, in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you stressed to Mr. Prstojevic the detrimental public relations impact of such efforts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to persuade him, Mr. Tieger, to impress it upon him that this was not to be done, it is not the done thing. I talked about the public -- the politics of the Serbian government, of the Serbian leadership, who kept repeating that one could not aspire after an ethnically-clean state in the space of Europe or the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. On Thursday, we spoke about specific individuals, that man from the Krajina, I cannot remember his name right now, and about Prstojevic, who were right-wingers, who were chauvinists, nationalists, which is a phenomenon in any nation. Yes, the man's name is Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as far as you could tell and during that conversation, Mr. Prstojevic understood the public relations aspect and assured you that he hadn't done so publicly; correct? In fact, he was at pains to make the point that he hadn't said that in public?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger. He didn't understand it to be for the sake of the public. He asked me, Who told you that? Where was this said, where was this heard? Who could have conveyed his positions to the government? There was no reference to the public, in the sense of the mass media, but this was said in front of another person who had relayed his position to the government, and, therefore, we ask him not to do what he was doing and what he was intending to do. There is another intercept of my conversation with Tomo Kovac, when I proposed to Tomo to try and persuade this Prstojevic not to do some things which he was stubbornly carrying out. I even proposed that if he could not do anything else, that he kill him. Of course, I wasn't being serious, but what I meant was that he should try, in every conceivable way, to try and persuade that person not to do that, what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In light of the information that you had, was there any effort made by you or anyone else to relieve Mr. Prstojevic of his responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In precisely this conversation, I explained to Prstojevic that it wasn't mine, as the minister of justice, to regulate the municipal administration. He could have only been dismissed from work by the local government, the local municipal president, the municipal administration. Possibly, the government could have introduced provisional measures and installed a caretaker municipal government, disbanding the former one, and thereby that could have been achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I assume the answer to this question flows from the first, but was there any effort made to initiate proceedings or to otherwise punish Mr. Prstojevic for what he had done or attempted to do?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what ground, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Distinguished Mr. Tieger says that he attempted to do something, but this was only said somewhere. We don't know for sure whether something was really done. We had a propaganda from the Muslim mass media that that was done, but Prstojevic, himself, denied having done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's not a proper intervention, Mr. Karadzic. You can clarify, if necessary, during your cross-examination. Mr. Mandic, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be so kind as to repeat the question, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there any effort, to your knowledge, made to initiate proceedings or to otherwise punish Mr. Prstojevic for what he had done or attempted to do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I received from Mr. Djeric information and an order to talk to Prstojevic and to point out to him that if he was doing those things, that he cannot do them. I don't know whether he was punished, I mean Prstojevic, in any way. He was a deputy to the Assembly and had such immunity, and he also was an official in the municipality. Whether he was punished, I don't know. I know that he was called to Pale after some time for a conversation to be conducted with him precisely in connection with those problems, but what happened after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I should stand corrected if I'm wrong, but Mr. Prstojevic was at the time the president of Serb municipality of Ilidza as well as an MP of the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can it be said that he, Mr. Prstojevic, as such, is a subordinate to you, you in the wider sense, as government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was an MP, Prstojevic, and he enjoyed immunity, Your Honour. The Executive Branch didn't have any powers vis-a-vis him until his immunity was waived by the municipality or, rather, by the Legislative Commission of the Serbian People, and, as such, he did not fall under the powers of the Executive Branch of government. This is a process whereby a deputy's immunity is waived in the National Assembly, and once that has been done by the Assembly, any proceedings can be instituted against him. Up to that point, as an MP enjoying immunity, like all the other MPs, and the president of the Assembly and the president of the state, he was immune to any such action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, you can say that he had immunity as to what he was doing in the capacity of the deputy of the Assembly, but I don't believe that he enjoyed such privilege in the capacity of the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he was concurrently an MP and the president of the municipality. At the same time, he held two offices. As an MP, he had been elected by the local people or by the deputies to the office of president of Ilidza municipality. By his very election to the office of president, his election to the office of president did not mean that his term of office, his mandate as a deputy, had seized. And in this conversation, I told him, It is not mine to order anything to you, but I am asking you, do not do that, because it is not good for the Serbian people, it is not in the interests of the Serbian people and its government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, this intercept was dated in June sometime, 2nd of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, how what the president of the municipality appointed at that time? Was he elected or appointed by somebody? How was the president of the municipality appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The MPs of the local Parliament elected the president of the Assembly, and the local parliamentarians elected him as the president of Ilidza municipality, the parliamentarians from the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, Mr. Mandic. My recollection is there was a discussion about Mr. Prstojevic during the discussion of the Krajisnik case, during which you indicated that he was a deputy, and that was later clarified in the course of your examination, that he was not. And that can be checked, of course, but that's my recollection, that you indicated that he wasn't a deputy. And, of course, we can check the records one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do check, Mr. Tieger I believe that he was among the 83 MPs of the 1st Serbian Assembly. I'm convinced of it. If I am wrong, I will be corrected, but I'm sure that he was an MP and that he came to Assembly sessions and spoke at Assembly sessions, as far as I can recall. In fact, I'm certain of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that he spoke at Assembly sessions. In fact, we looked, during the course of your testimony here, at some comments by Mr. Prstojevic at the 17th Assembly Session. But it's true, is it not, that others, beyond members of Parliament or deputies, spoke at the Assembly sessions, including ministerial officials, members of the Presidency, presidents of municipalities, and so on; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, in the parliamentary system, Assembly sessions are attended by the MPs, by the members of the government, and by the Presidency members, and at invitation, some other persons who the president of the Assembly deems should be present and contribute to the discussion. As Prstojevic was there every single time, I am convinced that he, indeed, was an MP, because there was no other grounds for him to be there. After all, find the list of the 83 members of Parliament, then, and there you will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've concluded. Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, one housekeeping matter. You are minded to tender all those exhibits designated as associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber had the opportunity to go through those items, and there are certain items, mainly intercepts, which are, in the view of the Chamber, not forming an indispensable or inseparable part of the witness transcript. So I will give you the numbers. Those are -- there are several: 20992, 30170, 30341, 30651, 30656, 30695, 30705, 30738, 30798, 30813, and 30833. Those intercepts were not played during the testimony of Mr. Mandic. Give me a minute. Those were simply admitted based upon the agreement of the parties, and the witness did not testify to this in the courtroom. And what the witness did was he authenticated a number of intercepts during his interview with the Prosecution. So in the Chamber's view, it does not form an indispensable or inseparable part of the transcript, so if you are minded to tender them separately, you have to deal with them item by item. I note the time. The Chamber should conclude today's hearing at quarter to 2:00, as usual, so we'll take a break now for 20 minutes. If you are minded, I would allow to go through with these items. Otherwise, Mr. Karadzic will begin his cross-examination. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, what I forgot to tell you is that the others will be admitted. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. In the interests of time, I'd like to direct the witness's attention to only one of the proposed exhibits that the Court mentioned. That's 20992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I may have devised or identified a way to expedite or speed up this process. I want to show you a particular document that was created during the course of the Krajisnik case. It will be up on screen in a moment. And if we could also show the witness the preceding page. Mr. Mandic, although this is in English, I know on the subsequent page you'll be able to identify the names in Latin script, but I thought it helpful to read to you this portion which indicates: "On October 1st, 2004, Momcilo Mandic listened to the following intercepted telephone conversations and identified voices of the participants as indicated below." And then if we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the e-court, this is page 1. The previous one is page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this indicates a number of intercepted telephone conversations, Mr. Mandic, including some of which you had an opportunity to listen to during the course of your testimony over the last few days. The headings are: The date of the conversation, the numbers that they're identified by in both B/C/S and English, the voices which were ID'd, and then, finally, the last heading is the interview transcript reference, that is, the portion of the interview in which you participated during which you identified those intercepts, according to this. So I simply wanted to confirm with you that you participated in a process, prior to your testimony in the Krajisnik case, during which you listened to intercepted telephone conversations and identified the voices.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would tender this document, and we will be in a position, therefore, I hope, to use it to the extent that some of these conversations may play a role in a subsequent submission following the appearance of a further submission related to the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're minded to tender only this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't asked Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson as to the other associated exhibit as well as this one. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted, and the exhibit number will be circulated to the parties by the Registrar in due course. Very well, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, please, let's begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Minister.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With the permission of the Court, I would like to express my compassion to you because of all the suffering you underwent on account of me, as did my family and friends, and many other persons who I don't even know, but they did suffer on my account. So please accept my apology because of what others did to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, on transcript page 404 -- or, rather, 4404, you say, on line 15: [In English] "In 2003, I was suspected of aiding and abetting and hiding Dr. Karadzic. I spent five months because of that in a solitary confinement cell in Belgrade, and none of my family members could visit me." [Interpretation] That's what you said; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President. No one was allowed to visit me, except for investigators from The Hague Tribunal, who came to the district prison in Bacvanska Street. They took me to separate rooms and they asked me about your health, your place of residence, who was financing you, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, on page 4405, you said: [In English] " ... that I was kidnapped as a citizen of Montenegro and transferred, in the space of two hours, to at prison in Sarajevo, without any extradition proceedings or anything else." [Interpretation] Further on, same page: [In English] "These operatives, the investigators, told me that I would be taken to court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that the prosecutor of the BiH Court would raise an indictment against me, and that I would be sentenced to a prison term of eight years. When I said that they had no grounds for filing a lawsuit against me, they said that they would find grounds and that wasn't important." [Interpretation] That's what these investigators of the OTP said to you; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, they kept all of their promises. As a citizen of the state of Montenegro, I was kidnapped without any proceedings whatsoever, extradition proceedings, nothing. I was kidnapped from my apartment and taken across the border. So I was met by Mr. Rattel at the border. He is one of the associates of The Hague OTP. Then I was at the Central Prison. Then I was taken to the detention unit of the BH Court. In the evening, as confirmed by the president of that Court, I was taken out by investigators, or, rather, operatives of the OTP from The Hague. Andan [phoen], Dragan, was with them then, the then chief of the Serb police. Again, they asked me about you, your health, your residence, everything else. And they said to me then that if I co-operate, that I would be back home very soon; if not, they would find some kind of indictment to issue against me. They would convict me, they would issue an indictment for war crimes. And I said, You have no grounds for any of that. I was here as a suspect several times. I think that Mr. Tieger was in charge of that investigation. My file was archived as one where there were no grounds to prosecute. In the evening, they kept all their promises. Privredna Banka is a bank that I own, and there was this case in that connection. Allegedly, that bank gave credit to some entities that were financing you. I was also indicted -- actually, I think that I'm the only man who was officially indicted for aiding and abetting suspects and accused persons by The Hague. I was freed of all charges because Toby Robinson gave false testimony. She appeared as an expert witness. I was charged because of these credits. Once I had served two-thirds of my sentence, it was established that that was nonexistent, that all of this had been stage managed. However, you know, Mr. President, that in Bosnia-Herzegovina US citizens have immunity and they cannot be prosecuted, not even for perjury. Ms. Robinson actually took some money from my bank as well, and she went to Dallas, Texas. There is another thing I have to say. The then high representative of the European Union for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Schwarz-Schilling on a Friday, extended Toby Robinson's term as provisional manager of my bank for an indefinite period of time. Sreten Jovic, who was then chief of police at the level of BH, and Sinisa Karan [phoen], brought documentation concerning all the mis-doings of that witness. I assume that Mr. Schwarz-Schilling first consulted Bonn, his government, that is. He thanked Toby Robinson for her co-operation, and she went back to the United States in an express manner. These are the people who detained me, turned me into a controversial businessman, whatever else, all of that because the suspicion was that I was helping you hide and that I was taking care of you and your health.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I be allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I understand those are all important to you, but the accused has only a limited time, so could you be brief in your answers. And both of you are speaking the same language, so I would like you to bear in mind to put a pause between the question and answers. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I be allowed to put to the Trial Chamber what kind of lawlessness we can live in? It is not only the high representative there who is authorised to do whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Come to your relevant question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that they put it well. If you don't do anything, you are given an eight-year term, and if you did something, then you get ten years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to complain to Mr. Tieger in any way? Wasn't he in charge of investigations in that case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as Sarajevo and Bosnia, Mr. Tieger never showed up. I did not have any contact with him. However, there were investigators from The Hague Tribunal there, or, rather -- yes, the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to try to put questions that will allow for brief yes-or-no answers, for a while, at least. In the Krajisnik case, did you have similar pressure exerted against you, and did you testify under such pressure; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the time, I was a suspect, I was a war crimes suspect. And, of course, Mr. Tieger's associates, Milford, I think the person's name was, and there were two of them, they kept notifying me of that, that I am a suspect, that I will probably be indicted, that I should watch what I'm saying. However, Mr. Tieger did his job, he was professional, he was fair, but he had these associates who were very aggressive and who kept putting it to me that I would probably be accused here. That was in 2004, after I had left solitary confinement in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were freed of all charges in the Bosnian Court for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything happened in accordance with the promises the investigators gave me. They said that I would be indicted, but that I would not be convicted. And that's what happened. I think that I was also charged with crimes against humanity and, yes, it was a final judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to take these little breaks, we have to make these little breaks. Now, I want to put something else to you, in addition to that pressure under which you testified in the Krajisnik case. We have admitted that transcript. On the 15th of December, 2004, Mr. Stewart said: [In English] "We have examined important witnesses, in our submission, in other [indiscernible]. We have done our best not to make that too obvious." [Interpretation] You testified on the 23rd of November, up until the 10th of December, 2004. Obviously, that has to do with you as well. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I testified at that time. As for these details, Mr. President, I really cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, on the 28th of February, 2005, Ms. Lucas [phoen] said: [In English] "With witnesses that go beyond the crime base into the critical linkage area, and this is the area, of course, in which the agreed-facts process broke down, the fact that we have not had a comprehensive reading and analysis of the relevant and potentially relevant documents means that our cross-examination in the Prosecution case is hampered."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly move into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall I hear you before we go into private session, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, the accused is inquiring about statements made by counsel after the appearance of this witness. This will call for -- not only is it now calling for various forms of speculation, but its relevance to this witness's testimony has not been made out, and I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Tieger's observations, in my judgement, are absolutely accurate. Mr. Mandic may have issues that he wishes to air, but your time is limited and these are not matters that go to the indictment against you. And then the question for the witness: Mr. Mandic, are you saying that your testimony in Krajisnik was inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. What I knew and what I said was correct in the Krajisnik case. It was the truth. That was in 2004. I think it was the second half of 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I should like to make a nexus with the last testimony of Mr. Mandic's which is obviously not associated with these pressures brought to bear upon him in the Krajisnik case. So I'm going beyond those pressures and the context in the Krajisnik case, because Mr. Mandic was not all that precise always then. That is as far as that is concerned. If you do not want to hear what Steward said in closed session in the Krajisnik case, that is okay, but please do tell me whether that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll hear the case. We'll go into private session, and let's see what the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, did you notice any difference in cross-examinations in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case relative to the cross-examination in the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were no longer under duress and that this Defence was more prepared than that of Krajisnik, did you notice that it was more fluent and more accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I'm sorry. That calls for -- first of all, it's irrelevant to the issues that this witness has to deal with in respect of you. Secondly, it calls for speculation. Thirdly, if it was allowed, it would open up such an issue that would have to be the subject of satellite litigation, that we would be wasting weeks, if not months. So please concentrate on those matters which are relevant to the indictment against you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, was that the subject you wanted to address us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's conclude with this: Would you add something to your testimony or change anything to your testimony in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I fully stand by my assertions in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In view of the fact that this is a Court witness, the Defence proposes that this reply be also tendered under 92 ter, and this was by way of introduction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, the interpreter is unable to keep up. Could the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to follow you in terms of numbers. Do you mean to tender the evidence of Mr. Mandic in the case of Zupljanin and Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These are D numbers, 1D -- under 1D that are being offered by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a general proposition, we, of course, have no objection to the use of 92 ter when it's properly perfected. I have to note here, however, that one of the elements of a 92 ter submission is the review of the statement that is being tendered, and that has not taken place yet. Indeed, I'd note that in the context of the 92 ter submission in Stanisic/Zupljanin, the Prosecution was required to translate the entirety of the transcript. So, again, I don't have objections, in principle, to the use of 92 ter by the other party, clearly, but I think it's important to note that the elements of 92 ter haven't been fulfilled here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was the Prosecution required to translate the entirety of the transcript, I mean, in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of the Krajisnik testimony, because the witness -- it wasn't clear whether the witness had listened to the entirety of the transcript, so he was sent back with the -- and the English transcript in that case was translated and provided to him for review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not in terms of disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, not for that purpose. For the specific purpose of review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter. But in the meantime, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's just one additional point of information. If the Chamber considers it necessary that this element be satisfied, we would ask that they make available the tapes of that testimony, and perhaps over the weekend he could review them and then be in a position next week to fulfill that requirement, if it's considered to be necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My technical question would be whether the witness should be put to cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: After Dr. Karadzic finishes, simply on the Zupljanin/Stanisic transcripts? I don't think we would have any objection if there was any matter in those transcripts that were covered by the testimony that wasn't covered by Dr. Karadzic in his own examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, the Defence has those audios.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it is inappropriate, but may I? I was given by Ms. Korner a translation of my testimony in the Krajisnik case, and it jogged my memory. That was six years ago. As regards the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, there is no need for that, because that was done a couple of months ago here and it is still fresh in my memory. So in my view, there is no need for my memory to be jogged in terms of what I had said in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case. That is my personal position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. And if asked, you would answer the same questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, definitely, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Answer the question in the same manner, I meant. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise, because I'll be asking you some basic questions, which I have to do for the benefit of the Chamber and the participants to be able to understand. Do you agree that in our system, and before the multi-party system, there had existed a legal obligation, and it was good practice that in the government there was an equal share of all the three nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they participated on an equal footing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that, in a way, there always had been some dominance of one coalition over another, even in that kind of a system, even in that system? Let me be of some assistance. If we go from Turkish times, when, as Zulfikarpasic puts it, we were a second-rate nation, but the Muslims were privileged; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were the majority nation, and they were in a position of some dominance in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And after a shorter rebellion, during the time of Austro-Hungary, they were also privileged?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I shall summarise it for you, and you can tell us what you think about it. During World War I, they were against the Serbs, the majority of them; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were -- the Muslim nation, as such, was part of the independent station of Croatia, and they also were members of the army of that state which had been created by Hitler and which was in existence until 1944.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that after the Second World War, they were in a coalition with the Serbs, and the Croats didn't have the best of times in Bosnia and Herzegovina because they had lost the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter's comment: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not overlap, Mr. Mandic and Mr. Karadzic. The interpreters have a very hard time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that; you were a younger man?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't know that. I was on the police force since age 15, and I didn't pay any attention to those kinds of things. And I don't know anything about that postwar period, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that as of the late 1960s, B and H was jocosely interpreted as the private store of Branko and Hamdija? Was there a dominance of the Croat and Muslim coalition in that time, the late 1960s?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that also in that system, involved the police and the judiciary and everywhere else, we had excellent professionals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that there were incorrect ideologically fervent people who persecuted other people on an ideological basis, on ideological grounds?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case throughout the history of the Yugoslav peoples, including after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree -- do you agree that in 1990, at the elections, the political system was changed from a mono-party system to a multi-party system?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the question of trust in the old personnel cadre could have been based on this ideological zealotry or inappropriateness in the previous system, or could a difference, could a distinction have been made between an appropriate suitable policeman and another policeman who acted on the basis of his ideological convictions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to put this to you: If somebody from the field does not agree to a certain appointment, is against it, am I right if I say that the grounds for such a displeasure can be: A, that in the previous system that person was unprofessional and ideologically incorrect; secondly, that that person was corrupt and associated with crime; thirdly, that he was subjected or subject to manipulation by Croats and Muslims; and, fourthly, that this fell into the category of personal dislike or personal animosity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Mr. President, in the socialist system, there was an entirety service, as well as individual policemen, who were actually socialism enthusiasts and who persecuted, in a way, people who were religious and who thought differently, and people who thought that the mono-party system, i.e., socialism, was not a good system. And those people would, as a rule, be persecuted or would stand criminal trial, or would in other ways be driven from the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As regards these other categories that you mentioned, it is true that there were unprofessional people, corrupt people, manipulated people, that there had been personal antagonisms between the local party bosses and the people who were to remain or be appointed to these work posts that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if somebody from the field asked for an appointment not to be made, we could assume that the reason for that would have been one of these four grounds that I mentioned. Do you remember that we actually did not acknowledge this fourth basis, the personal animosity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said so, and I have repeatedly stated that, at least as far as you are concerned, Mr. President. Mr. Tieger has managed to present to us two intercepts over this period of a year between you and me and between me and Thomas [as interpreted]. There were various pressures from the field for certain appointments of certain persons to be made. I'm not only referring to the Serbian side, but also for the Muslim and the Croat side. But you never asked -- nobody ever personally asked me to settle unsettled interpersonal relations before that period in this way, namely, but not by not appointing such a person. At least I personally do not know of any such instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you perhaps, by any chance, remember that after the -- immediately after the elections, I immediately proposed the setting up of an expert rather than a party government in order to ease political tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
