utterances.text: I know that you proposed the setting up of an expert government, but when that was or whether before or after -- when after the elections, I cannot recall with precision, Mr. President, because I was at the court and I was not au courant with the political goings on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you to jog your memory the names of the persons of the Serbian Democratic Party had appointed to executive branch positions because they had one executive power, would you be able to identify them? Do you know who the ministers and the deputy ministers of the Serbs were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know all the personnel structure, I know all the people, because I co-operated with them throughout 1991 and in early 1992, as well as later; namely, those people who became part of the Government of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the justice minister was Ranko Nikolic, and in the previous system he was set up as allegedly guilty of a corruption affair, and we gave him his job back?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the justice minister of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the first one in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that he was not an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I could tell you about two persons called Pejic, Momcilo and Zdranko Pejic. They are related, in a way. Momcilo was also a minister in one of the governments of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the Government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Momcilo Pejic was not a member of any party, and he was the finance minister of the government before the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We also appointed him finance minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Zdranko Pejic, also as an expert and as an economist, was part of the Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that none of these people, not Miodrag Simovic, nor the minister of agriculture and forestry, Nadazdin, nor the deputy health minister, Dr. Tatjana Starevic, Medan, none of the others were SDS members, apart from the late Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to begin with myself, I was never a member of the SDS, and I was elected as police minister for the Serbian people. And most of these people had no party affiliation in the first multi-party government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have already confirmed that you and I did not know each other before, and do you know that I didn't know Zepinic or Simovic, either, before the government was formed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer to that. But as far as I'm concerned, I saw you for the first time in my life, I believe, in early 1991, when Vito Zepinic brought me to the party offices to nominate me for this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that none of the regional police chiefs was a party member and I didn't know them personally?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember, at our first meeting you told me, You are Mr. Mandic, after the introductions, You are a judge? I answered, Yes. And you said, Please, if you come to occupy that post, please, together with Zepinic, appoint only professional policemen who are of Serb ethnicity and fitting for that post. That remains etched in my memory because that was my first encounter with you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Who are of Serb ethnicity and are fitting for the post that is allocated to the Serb community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you are aware of the method of appointment of Mr. Zupljanin, of the way he was appointed. There had been a longstanding crisis there. Zupljanin and I attended together a meeting, and most of the SDS was in favour of an honourable judge. And I asked, Who was the more professional of the two? And after hearing the answer, I chose Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that, but I know it was at Zepinic's proposal that the chief of police in Banja Luka was appointed, Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that I was exposed to critique and pressure by party members, who said that the party had won power at the elections, but I didn't give party members power, favouring experts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was also criticised for appointing Muslims and some of my Serbs, as they said in the police, favouring them over various nominees by various national parties, and they were very rough in their insistence that party people come to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Serbian Democratic Party did not take the chance to take over any of their power ministries, as they called them, the Ministry of the Interior and the Defence Ministry; we chose, instead, the Finance Ministry, the Ministry of Information, the Ministry of Agriculture, Water Management and Forestry? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The Defence Ministry was taken by the Croats, as coalition parties, and the minister was Jerko Doko. The minister of police went to the majority party, the Muslim party. Alija Delimustafic was the minister of police. And the Finance Ministry was headed by Pejic and others, who had taken over from the previous regime, who were experts and who continued in their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that it was a very good custom, even during Socialist times, and also under the law and under the inter-party agreement, it was agreed that senior posts be allocated in such a way that if post number 1 in a certain field goes to one party, then the post number 2 goes to the second majority party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to explain that to Mr. Tieger. If, let's say, the Serbs were in the majority in a certain place, the chief of police would be a Serb. And if the second majority community was Croat, then a Croat would be man number 2, that is, police commander in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In one of these intercepts that we are going to tender to be marked for identification, I inform one of you that in Prijedor, in addition to the police chief and police commander, posts that belonged to Serbs, they had appointed a Muslim, and there was also a Muslim as secretary of defence in that municipality, et cetera. Was that a matter that could be of concern to another community? It was not only unfair, but it was also worrisome?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you remind me? What was that document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will go through documents one by one. 65 ter, please, 18004. This is a 65 ter document that should have a translation. This is a letter from the Serbian Democratic Party, dated 7 March 1991, addressed to all municipality boards of the SDS, and the subject is "The procedure for selecting executive personnel within the competencies of republic ministries." It says: "Appointments for chiefs of the Security Services Centre and commanders shall follow this procedure: The Municipal Assembly or the Executive Board of the municipality puts forward an official nomination, with prior inter-party agreement, to the Ministry of the Interior, and the minister -- and Vito Zepinic, deputy minister. Please do not exert pressure to appoint candidates who do not meet the requirements, and it is desirable to nominate two candidates for each post." And then I have a separate proposal concerning the justice minister. The appointments should be decided by the government. Could the witness please see page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with what you know about the position of the Serbian Democratic Party; namely, that the procedure be observed strictly and that only the government could decide, and that there should be two candidates for each post?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, there were only three nominations made in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. At least two, but usually three. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We don't have the translation for this document, so it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D355, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now get 65 ter 18554.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Minister, let me inform you. This is an allocation of various executive posts in ministries between parties. The first -- I seem to be reading very fast for the interpreters. I hope you see it on the screen. You see the post of the minister goes to the HDZ in the Defence Ministry, deputy minister is from the SDA, et cetera. But what you know better is the Ministry of the Interior. Can you see, from this, that we got the deputy minister post and then the assistant minister for crime prevention - that was you - Zepinic was a deputy minister, and then you also got -- we also got the post of the assistant minister for analysis and information. Is it the case, let me ask you, that in the Ministry of the Interior, the minister is the most important position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the second-ranking post the chief of State Security?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that we only got deputy positions for both these posts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the minister or someone in the Ministry of the Interior unlawfully abolished the post of under-secretary for state security, which was to have gone to us?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember, Mr. President, before Mr. Kvesic's deputy was to take up his post from the ranks of the Serbian people, and it was to be Nedjo Vlaski, a man who had served in the security system in the Socialist regime, with many years of service, Branko Kvesic made a new staffing system and practically deleted this post of deputy. So the Serbian Democratic Party lost this executive position, and you protested against this more than once. You wrote a series of letters, and, nevertheless, Nedjo Vlaski never took up that post which was to have gone, according to the inter-party agreement, to the Serbian community. That is the same Branko Kvesic to whom we have listened in an intercept presented by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, are you aware -- were you aware of this document? For example, whose handwriting is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is Mr. Karadzic's handwriting. I think; I'm not sure. We had all this in the ministries and in the government, this allocation of posts document, to be able to know which post had to go to which community. This is a document that reflects the inter-party agreement, the coalition agreement between the parties that had won the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you seeing a date in this document? Probably the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] January 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just two quick things, Your Honour. I think the need for the Court to intervene arose because it appears to me to be a process by which the accused tries to authenticate the document and then proceeds to ask questions about it generally. I think we need to -- he'll need to concentrate more on the possibility of the witness doing so. Secondly, I'm not aware whether there's a translation for this, but beyond the procedural irregularity, I don't have an objection to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll mark that for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D356, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you need to put the foundation material to the witness so that the Chamber can understand the document, what it is about. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would only like to say this:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, does this reflect the gist of the inter-party agreement, according to which executive authorities should have acted in making appointments?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the viewpoint of the SDA and the HDZ, the representatives of Muslims and Croats respectively, was everything honoured?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Ministry of Police is concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were Serbs cheated out of this post of deputy under-secretary for state security by virtue of this unlawful modification of the staffing system, the staffing specification?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know well what state security meant in our system. Could that have been a reason for concern among the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you make that question a bit clearer? Which Serbs, those employed with the police, or the party, or all Serbs in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All of them, in general. Do you agree that State Security was an important branch that could control practically everything, especially under the previous system?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the State Security Branch, the security of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this method, first post to one community, the second to another community, was established to achieve democracy in the control system?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that in the State Security Branch, this mechanism of democratic control was breached by cancelling this post that was to have gone to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could that have been a reason for concern for Serbs employed in the police, those in the party, and Serbs, in general?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about the people, in general, or even the employees in the police. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, if things were happening as they were in Croatia, do you agree that the very roots of the secessionist armies in Slovenia, Croatia, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, were in the MUPs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that State Security in Bosnia and Herzegovina belonged to the HDZ, was allocated to the HDZ, the representatives of the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they in favour of secession, and were they on the side of Croatia in the war against Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From that point of view, then, if State Security were not to have that kind of control, such as deputy under-secretary for state security from the ranks of the Serbs would have been, would that be a reason for concern?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, for the SDS and for the leadership of the SDS, the people probably didn't know about all of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 30020. Could we have that, please? It is an intercept. We have to use it, although we have objections in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 21st of May, 1992. This is a conversation between Mr. Zepinic and myself. Do you agree that at that point in time, Zepinic was, by definition and in terms of the office he held, responsible for the appointment of Serb personnel to appropriate positions that belonged to the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vito Zepinic was a member of the Serb Democratic Party, in the Ministry of Police.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the witness is directed to particular portions of the intercept, could we have a bit more clarification of what the objections are to the intercept? We have to use it, although we have objections in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably, he was referring to his general objections he referred to in one of his earlier submissions. Am I correct, Mr. Karadzic, in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to establish, with the assistance of this document, how the realisation took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I meant your objections to the intercepts you referred to in your statement. You said: "It is an intercept. We have to use it, although we have objections in that regard." What objections did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, our well-known position that was presented by Mr. Robinson as well; namely, that these intercepts, before the war, can only be used as evidence for the unfairness of the SDA that is unlawfully tapping all the conversations of Serbs, and not Muslims and Croats. We could not get a single intercept of Alija Izetbegovic or any other party leader or state official from the Muslim side; also, Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, all the rest. That is to say, if they are taken as evidence, they can only be taken as evidence proving that the Serb side was under unlawful pressure there. But they were listening in, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you satisfied?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, Mr. Mandic did not say that Vito Zepinic was a member of the Serb Democratic Party. He was not a member of the Serb Democratic Party. The witness did not say that. He was the personnel officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He took care of that to see that the inter-party agreements are honoured properly on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he took care of the personnel policy on behalf of the SDS in the Ministry of the Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will go back to see who the candidates were and according to which criteria. Can we now have page 2 of this document. In Serbian, I see it -- ah, I see, yes. I'm not sure that the English and Serbian versions are the same. What I'm saying here is: "What about the special unit?" In Serbian, it is the first box on this page. Obviously, I had realised that something was being changed in the special unit. And further down, it says: "If they got the police command, then we would have to get the command of the special unit." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A bit further down, I'm expressing my concern because in Vojkovici -- Vojkovici is a Serb neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that some people in civilian clothes are snooping around Vojkovici, there are 20 of them, and it is obvious that they are policeman, but in civilian clothes. Zepinic says: "Para-state?" I say: "I don't know whether it is para-state. I'm afraid it is not the police, because there seems to be no distinction there ." Did you notice that immediately after the elections, there was less and less of a distinction between the SDA and the police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ministry of Police, the chief of the uniform police was from the ranks of the Muslim people. Ex officio, he was the superior of the special unit of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, was a Croat, Vikic, the commander of this special unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be proper, if the chief of the police is a Muslim, that the head of that unit should be a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that, Mr. President, because Vito Zepinic was in charge of personnel policy at the time and I was not really very well-versed, as far as these discussions were concerned at ministry level, in terms of pursuing personnel policy within the Ministry of Police.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, please, this entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, if you see that, it has to do with my dissatisfaction over the way in which Vito Zepinic is carrying out the inter-party agreement, and I'm asking him why there are some people who the people from local level do not want. Do you see that? It is here on this page, and I am asking about some Maletic, and so on and so forth. Do you agree that the most frequent problem was that at local level they did not want anyone who had been persecuting them in the previous system unlawfully?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, that we took care of that when we discussed those four positions; lack of corruption, manipulation, and so on. Right now, you are talking about those individuals who persecuted Serbs who were not eligible in the times of socialism. You are presenting that to Zepinic, who is explaining certain things to you and the way in which he sees the election of these people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 5 in English. I believe that in Serbian, it would be page 4. Yes, it is page 4 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what I say here is: "First there is a Croat, I think, and the second one, too. Please, let us take that, because they have the police command, they have this Hebib. We should at least take that so that our people can be sure that nothing illegal would be done. We are not afraid of anything that is legal, but we are afraid that something illegal would be done." Have you found that particular box?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've just reminded me, Mr. President. The commander of the brigade of the special unit was a Croat. The commander of the special unit was also a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you found that box. So what we are asking for is democratic control, that it is impossible for the knife and the bread to be in the same hand, as we say in our part of the world; that is to say, that the number-one and number-two man cannot be from the ranks of the same people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was insisted upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the next box is what I am saying: "And then -- and then when we have our own man there, then he can guarantee that there will be nothing illegal. And, finally, it is only fair that it is equal everywhere. If our man is in charge, they will have a deputy, and if it is theirs, we will have the deputy, and that will be okay. Okay, you're going to take care of that." And so on and so forth. Do you agree that for a considerable amount of time, we believed that Mr. Zepinic would take care of this, and finally it turned out that we were unsatisfied because Mr. Zepinic was subject to manipulation, people on the ground were dissatisfied?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted; for identification, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D357.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2019, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Mandic, let me ask you: Do you recall that the government was established sometime towards the end of January 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, since we were in a position to know, that already in February 1991 a decision had been passed to establish a council for the defence of Muslims attached to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that it started functioning already in the month of June?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us take care of this first. Do you recall the document? We don't have the Serbian version on our screen. I don't have it either. It's the 4th of June, 1991. The Ministry of the Interior is sending this document to the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. Do you remember that Mrs. Plavsic was chairman of this counsel?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Biljana Plavsic was president of the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have this document in B/C/S, Your Honours? I don't have it, but you can read it out, and then you're going to realise what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report on the arrest of members of the Croatian MUP. It's from 1992, actually, but -- all of it is 1991, the 18th of May, 1991. And on the 4th of June, 1991, you are writing this accompanying letter to the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, when some men from the Croatian MUP were arrested, those who were transporting weapons through Bosansko Grahovo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, weapons and Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what this incident was all about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Public Security Station in Bosansko Grahovo stopped a convoy that was transporting weapons across the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia. There were rifles there, ammunition, and Motorolas. I am informing Ms. Biljana Plavsic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to read it out in English: [In English] "With regard to your request in letter strictly confidential number," so-and-so, "the 3rd of June, 1991, we are sending you the report of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of 18th May of 1991 on the arrest of members of the MUP of Republic of Croatia by the staff of Bosansko Grahovo Station -- Public Security Station, and the report of 27th of May, 1991, on the working meeting at which the question of ordering the detention and extending the detention of the three policemen from the Croatian MUP was reviewed." [Interpretation] That's all Ms. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, and I don't know how long Dr. Karadzic intends to spend with this document, but we can certainly provide a hard copy of the -- obviously, there's a B/C/S for this document. It was created in B/C/S. We can provide a hard copy to be put on the ELMO or e-mail it. But if he's going to read portions of it, that would obviously be quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean to go into detail, but it is going to be of interest to the participants. I would just like to have this confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Ms. Plavsic ask you, on the 3rd of June, to inform her, as head of the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, about this incident, and that on the 4th of June, you sent this letter with a report attached?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? If the witness wishes to refresh his memory, he can have a look at the Serbian version, but I'm not going to discuss it in depth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The date -- rather, the year on the second page should be a typo, Mr. Mandic. It should read "1991," I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was sent in 1991, Mr. Mandic; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that this was before the outbreak of conflicts in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time, Mr. Karadzic. If it's convenient, we'll have a break now for half an hour. Yes, Mr. Tieger, do you have something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just very quickly, Your Honour, with regard to the 92 ter issue related to Stanisic/Zupljanin. Obviously, I have no interest in being obstructive. Clearly, when you look at 92 ter -- well, I shouldn't say "clearly." Testimony transcribed and taken in open court presents somewhat different issues than statements. Nevertheless, we have the issues presented. It would have been a bit helpful if we'd been notified in advance so we could give some thought to that, but I'm not precluding the possibility that the Prosecution will get back with a position accommodating to the Defence. But I think we need a moment -- at least some opportunity to consider it, in light of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since you raised this, I was about to raise it after the recess, but given the page numbers are over 1.000, so instead of tendering the whole transcript in Stanisic/Zupljanin, I'm minded to tell the accused to identify specific parts of the transcript that he would wish to have admitted, whether the purpose of tendering is either to show the inconsistency of his statement or adding some parts to the evidence. With that, we'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you seemed to have something to say when I said about the transcripts of this witness in Stanisic and Zupljanin trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. That is about 440 pages. If that is much, then I can go through that transcript and we can have it confirmed by the witness. But I would, in that case, need an additional day for my examination. If I do get that day, if it is easier for the Chamber so that we do not encumber the entire case file, we can also proceed in that way, but I do have to have that additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While you can go along with the parts that you wish to put to the witness, please let us know those specific page numbers you have in mind, so then we can have a look and then can indicate in which way we should proceed. So if you could let the Chamber know, in writing or even through e-mail, whatever, or whatever means you find appropriate. Let us know the page numbers you -- specific page numbers you referred to, as 400 pages; be it 400 or 300, let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If we would not go through it in this way, it would be entire testimony of Mr. Mandic. But if we do get this time, we can go through it and clarify some points which the witness will then, on his part, corroborate or deny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't mean necessarily that you have to go through each item in order to tender them. What I told you, let the Chamber know in advance what page numbers you are minded to tender. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If I remember correctly, this document has been admitted, the one of the 4th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it has been admitted as Exhibit D358.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D1891.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, I believe that you -- at least as much as we knew about the clandestine actions of the Party of Democratic Action, but this is no secret; namely, on the 11th of June, in Sarajevo, was formed the SDA National Defence Council. Did you confirm that just a while ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to see that document, 1D -- yes, that is it. I don't know whether we have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that that document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The then general-secretary of the Party of Democratic Action is, in the signature line, Hasan Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When I said that the link between the SDA and the police was being lost, I was largely referring to, actually, Mr. Hasan Cengic. Do you know that Mr. Hasan Cengic is a minister of the faith, a hodja by profession?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know everything about Mr. Hasan Cengic. I worked in the service for a long time. I know that Mr. Cengic first completed the medresa and then the Theological Faculty either in Algeria or IN Iran. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that he was part of the group that, together with Alija Izetbegovic, was convicted by the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Court in 1983 of association on the basis of the Islamic Declaration?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of this group which was called the Young Muslims, and he was tried and convicted, together with Mr. Izetbegovic, in the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that his father, Halid, as early as in the -- as in 1990, before the elections, had formed the first unit of the Patriotic League in Foca and in the mosque in Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you know that his father was Halid, and that later he was the chief logistics officer of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we will see another document. Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D359.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D1885.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until that is shown on the screen, could I ask you this: Would it be fair to say -- well, we saw that Ms. Plavsic was the president of the Council for the Protection of The constitutional Order, but do you agree that the president of the Presidency is, by virtue of his office, the president of the Council for the Defence of the Republic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a constitutional category.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And was it Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I told you that Mr. Izetbegovic, in addition to being the president of the council for the defence of the entire republic, of -- for all the three nations, that is, becomes the president of the semi-legal clandestine council for the defence of just the Muslims? Whom should he arrest, I mean Mr. Izetbegovic, in such a role?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a witness here, Mr. President. I'm not an expert. When you call me as an expert, I can give you an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this that document -- there was another page in front. I don't know why it is missing right now. Can you take a look at this cover letter. Can you actually read it aloud, and can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In keeping with the joint agreement of authorised representatives of the MUP of the SR B&H and the MUP of the Republic of Croatia and the instructions on the manner of employing candidates at the Education Centre in the Republic of Croatia MUP, the Party of Democratic Action, Sarajevo, recommends the above-named candidates to attend a course at your centre. "Yours faithfully, acting SDA secretary, Hasan Cengic." This is Mirsad Lukovic. The person in question is Mirsad Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He signed on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, actually, Mirsad Lukovic is the person being assigned to the course, the name of the candidate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the name of the candidate is Mirsad Lukovic, but somebody signed on behalf -- the letter on behalf of Hasan Cengic, the SDA secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you now see -- this is the basic document, but we have 80 such applications for training in Croatia. Did there exist appropriate training in Bosnia-Herzegovina for training the police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there existed a number of places where the police were trained. Well, there was a training centre at Vraca where the regular secondary school cadets attended, and of the senior schools as well. And there were different courses for forensic technicians, for policemen, for anti-sabotage purposes and units, and such, so on and so forth. Also, there was a centre, a training centre, in Tarcin, in Banja Luka, in Bihac, in Mostar, and I believe also one in Doboj. That is as far as training courses for policemen are concerned, but I'm not quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To clarify it for the Chamber, these courses were for adults who had already had some educational backgrounds and were only being additionally trained to be policemen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the so-called specialist courses where people applied who had done their military service, who had completed one of the specialised secondary schools, if there were courses for policemen, for forensic technicians, for counter-sabotage defence, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In contrast to that, cadets would attend the Secondary Police School?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, pupils, cadets like I, myself, was, who attended for the four-year school, police school, secondary school at Vrace, from 815 to 19 mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These people that the SDA was assigning to Croatia for training, were they cadets or were they mature people of age who were to undergo this training for additional training, additional education?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were courses for probationers, for apprentice policemen, as it were, meaning that the already-formed persons attended these courses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see another cover letter on the ELMO, please, from the same field. It ought to be in e-court, but we cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to read this one out too?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Instruction for assigning candidates to the training centre of the Republic of Croatia, 11th July. To the Executive Board of the SDA, to the president. "Enclosed, we are attaching a copy of instructions on the manner of admitting -- of employing policemen in the MUP of the Republic of Croatia, with your obligation being to acquaint your candidates with these instructions. It is the duty of every candidate to take along a letter of recommendation by the party, which we are attaching here; also, his birth certificate, marriage certificate, and the birth certificates for family candidates, as well as a certificate on having completed a military service, a certificate of a clean police record, no prior convictions, a certificate of educational background and employment record and working booklet, if any, and, if they also should pass, a certificate on a medical checkup." And below it is the address of the Educational Centre in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hasan Cengic is in the signature, but also signed by somebody else on his behalf, and a greeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is a party document, like all the instructions in general are?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is by the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you say that there was no reason whatsoever for the party to be assigning people to be trained, the policemen or candidates for the police force to be trained in Croatia? It could have been done in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was without the knowledge of the Ministry of the Interior, and it was without the knowledge of any state organ in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you knew that, as any police would known?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We had information about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can I be a bit more clear? Can I be clearer? You said that was done without the knowledge of the Ministry of the Interior, and then you said you have -- you had had information about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Ministry of the Interior in Bosnia and Herzegovina had all its training centres and educational centres in which all profiles of policemen were trained, starting with specialist courses and through secondary schools up to universities. We had information from the field that in a clandestine fashion, members of the Muslim nationality were being sent to training courses in Croatia without the knowledge of the official Ministry of the Interior. This was never discussed, nor was the minister ever informed officially of this, or any one of us in the ministry, the members of the minister's collegium, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are welcome, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say, then, that this was actually the formation of a party police force behind the back of the regular state organ?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the Party of Democratic Action is secretly and behind their backs sending -- behind the backs of the state police sending people to be trained in another republic, is that an action whereby the Party of Democratic Action is creating its own armed force?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, we were not clear on what was happening. We -- the non-Muslim personnel in the Ministry of the Interior, we were not clear on whether they were being sent to the front in Croatia under the veil of training, or was it the intention for them to be trained there and then to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was only towards the end of 1991 and early 1992 that we found out what the objective of that training had been and of assigning young Muslims to not only Croatia and Zagreb but also to other Islamic countries for such training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will admit the previous document, i.e., 1D1885, as Exhibit D360. But I'm not sure about the status of the next document, another document of similar kind. Is it listed in 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be part of the same exhibit, because this is a cover letter, in a way, explaining the documents that were attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the date is the same, of similar kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll mark them for identification, pending translation, given the second part of the document was not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I just inform you that this text of the instructions is the same for 80-something candidates. One was translated, and just the names change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me ask you: When testifying in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, you had an opportunity of seeing these names of persons who were sent to Croatia. Were all of these names Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D1882, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, let me ask you: Were there any Muslims who were against this, who criticised it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, that happened when these young people returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina and when they were assigned to different jobs. Then certain officials, both at higher and lower levels who were of Muslim ethnicity and who were not familiar with this, were actually surprised; and they did not agree to having these people taken in, in spite of the fact that there were trained people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nevertheless, these other persons were admitted into the Ministry of the Interior. However, no one had known that these people were being trained.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1882, please, could we have that now. Let me say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you say whether it has been up-loaded?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it should be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm hearing, No, from the Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It should be released, I suppose. It is -- just a few seconds. [Interpretation] All right. While we're waiting for this, could we have 65 ter 30103. Well, we do have the previous one, yes, 1D1882. And 1883 should be in preparation. Yes, this is the English version. Can we have the Serbian version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I inform you that this is a letter from the Banja Luka Centre of Security Services to Ms. Plavsic, as president of the council. And it says up here: "To the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Let's not read all of it. Could you read the last paragraph down here, and then let's move on to the next page. Can you see this in Serbian? It starts with the words "Da se"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read that, and then we'll move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean, "On Monday, the 22nd of July ..." should I start from there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On Monday, the 22nd of July, 1991, I was at a meeting in the Ministry, and I could not believe my eyes when I received the survey of the staffing system. It was not so much the content that amazed me as the appearance, or, to be more precise, the colour in which it was printed. It is a well-known fact that the colour of police equipment is blue, so why, then, is green suddenly being introduced in official correspondence? And is this a sign of the dominance of Muslims in this important ministry? All of this was the doing of two assistant ministers: assistant minister for the police, Mr. Avdo Hebib, and assistant minister for legal and administrative matters and foreign nationals, Mr. Hilmo Selimovic. "That attempts were being made to create a Muslim army out of this Ministry is also apparent from --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... from this ministry is also apparent from the most recent police training course that began on the 22nd of July, 1991. Our recommendation was that if a course had to be organised, then, in accordance with the shortfall in numbers on the basis of ethnicity, the course should accept a larger number of Serbs from the Republic of Croatia who work in the security services there and are being subjected to the most perfidious methods, by means of which they are being driven out of the service. This would have significantly reduced the expenses of the course. However, a very perfidious game is being played over the admission of these course students. First, 300 candidates were recommended, and then 400 candidates. We have information to the effect that a significant number of the course students are Muslims from Sandzak (around 80 per cent) ... "

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... that some ethnic Muslims are being sent in an organised way to a course in the MUP of the Republic of Croatia. It is obvious from the Official Note that some ethnic Muslims are being sent in an organised way to --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber: Where is Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Republic of Serbia. It is the district of Raska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it rather customary to say Sandzaklija in Bosnia and Sarajevo, particularly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the name that is used for Muslims who come from the district of Raska and who live in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this document admitted, and then could we call up 1883.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be exhibited as -- admitted as Exhibit D361.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, now we have this document, that the chief of the Banja Luka Security Services is speaking. So this is an official note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at it? There's no need to read it out. Please don't read the names out. Let these persons remain anonymous, because that is what was intended. But, anyway, everyone can see it from the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could it please not be displayed to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see here that a police operative found out -- namely, that this gentleman informed him that Isak Gunic, nicknamed Isak, was going as an SDA member to a course that is organised in Zagreb, that he was going to be trained in Zagreb for two months, that he would be receiving a salary there of six and a half thousand dinars, and that this was being financed by the Arab Emirates. And then Gunic also showed them questionnaires that they were to supposed to fill out when going to Zagreb. This gentleman says the SDA was written in the title of the questionnaires and that the questionnaires were signed by Hasan Cengic. This Muslim said that he refused to go, and he informed his colleague, this policeman, who compiled this Official Note. Is this in keeping with what you found out unofficially about this illegal activity of the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the ways in which we found out about the fact that these young persons of Muslim ethnicity were being sent for training to the Republic of Croatia. I explained that a moment ago to the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me ask you: If the Party of Democratic Action is preparing a secret police, a secret armed force, who would be their assumed adversary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And possibly the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a people, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D362.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 30103. 30103. May I inform you that this is an intercept of a conversation taking place between myself and Mr. Krajisnik on the 13th of July, 1991. This conversation primarily relates to difficulties within the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that there's no such document in the e-court. Could you check it again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 65 ter number, 30103. It should be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have it. 65 ter 30103, I have it. It should be coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now please have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, we need page 2. It will be a good thing if we had the Serbian version as well, instead of this Official Note that we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says here. In the Serbian version, it's towards the bottom: "That Mico Stanisic called me," says Mr. Krajisnik. And then he goes on to say: "They are in serious trouble over there, and we simply must make a big cut. That Ljuto stung me again." I think it's really "Vito," not "Ljuto." "The other day, "let him -- well, go to hell." And I say: "Vito is a monster [as interpreted]." I don't know. "Rajko, we need to persuade Rajko that Vito is a monster," because Rajko had put him up as a candidate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page? In English, it's 3. I did not say "monster," I said "cudo," "miracle."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The right interpretation would be "quite a piece of work."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: See what it says here now? Well, Krajisnik says: "They have not resolved that. I thought that we should convene all the cadres that are there, and let us write this up along with all the irregularities and say, 'Gentlemen, let us resolve all of this, and we are simply looking for an answer. We want this to be resolved.' That is quite obvious." And so on and so forth. Now, perhaps it would be better if you would read one Krajisnik and one Karadzic and then --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says "ma ja." You can see that. It's the fourth line from the bottom -- or from the top.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Oh, yes, it's terrible, these petty deceits and tricks. I mean, it is contemptible. People cannot living together that way. It is terrible, what they're doing." Momo Krajisnik: "Yes, yes." Karadzic: "And Vito is there and helping them. Actually, they've bought him, man. They've given him a car. Now they're paying for his flat. They're all scum. He's a scumbag. I think he's the worst scumbag." Krajisnik: "Oh, my goodness. For my own sake, I can't believe what you're saying. But, honestly, this is no good."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what it is that the two of us are discussing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified in the Zupljanin/Stanisic case, I described in detail that the SDA had corrupted Mr. Vito Zepinic. And, Mr. President, when we were talking about that one category of people, that's where he was. He was given a car, Mazda 626, it was found in Kasindol, near Lukavica, at the beginning of the war. Also in the Street Leninova, number 8, they bought him a house, next door to the kindergarten called Bosko Buha; we know exactly where it was. And he also got some money. We found the Mazda and the house that was bought for his business premises. We just didn't find the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was supposed to be the service he was supposed to render? It wasn't really a house. The transcript says "house," but it is just business premises. That is to say that it can be a shop or some such premises where business transactions can take place.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, business premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why would they give such valuables to him? Why?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we all know, Vito Zepinic was the ranking Serb in the ministry. He was the personnel officer, and he was in charge of all of that that was happening in the ministry. Basically, the objective was for him to help the arming of the Muslim people, and that the weapons that came through Croatia and Slovenia, or, rather, by aeroplane from the Arab countries, enter Bosnia-Herzegovina unhindered. Inter alia, there were personnel problems. And also there were other honest people there whom they were trying to keep silent. For a while, I think that he had dazzled you, in a way, Mr. President, by some of these stories he made up about people who had actually carried out their work honestly through Rajko Dukic. He made an effort to stay there for as long as possible and to do the things that the SDA had paid him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at the next one after Krajisnik. I'm talking about Rajko. I say: "No. Rajko is here. Now he feels guilty because he had recommended him. He shouldn't feel guilty." Do you agree that we had all made mistakes in making various appointments and I'm trying to relieve Rajko Dukic of his feeling of remorse?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know it, Rajko Dukic used to be the president of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party, and he was the main personnel officer in the party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also see English page 5 and Serbian page 3. The next one in Serbian, and page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Throughout this conversation, we discussed the things that were going on and our inability to get the MUP to work lawfully. And look at this line where Krajisnik says: "Well, how ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Well, how? What did he mess up? Listen, I told that lot down there, 'Gentlemen, we have the right only to live together, and we will press for that, and we won't let anyone break up Bosnia at the expense of the Serbian people. That's it.'" Karadzic says: "Right." Krajisnik goes on: "So, on the whole, it's all right."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that we were working for a united, undivided Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state with the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this intercept be admitted? Now it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification as Exhibit D363. And there are a couple of additional administrative matters which first relates to the previous document, 1D1882. Noting that there's no translation for that, we will -- would mark that for identification as well. And then --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Zupljanin's letter to Plavsic. Did we -- no, no, this is the -- I'm sorry, the -- Pecanic's Official Note. I don't think there was one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1D -- so Exhibit -- is, then, the English translation for D362?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3. Not for 2, but 3. 1883.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So there's no English translation for 1D1883, so we'll mark it for identification, pending translation. And in relation to the 1D1885, which we admitted as Exhibit D360, marked for identification, when I checked the e-court while it was put to the witness, there was only one document, but I'm not sure whether Mr. Sladojevic played a measure or not. Now it consists of 80 documents, 80 cover letters. And then the one you showed through ELMO may be included in one of those documents. I haven't checked it. So we will admit only -- that being the case, we will admit only those two pages that were put to the witness. I don't see the necessity to admit all of them. So we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this is a standard letter of recommendation for all 80 of them. It's a standard format. We can have it admitted as such because it's the same text for all these people. Only the names change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we have evidence, and in the witness confirmation there are -- there were 80 of them. We don't have to admit them all. We don't need to then translate again. So we can proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now call up 65 ter 0113 [as interpreted]. I believe that it was already tendered during the cross-examination by the Prosecution. But on English page 4 I'd like you to look at -- the 65 ter is 30113. We don't have the right document now. 65 ter 30113. Maybe it's already in evidence. Now I'd like English page 4 and Serbian page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the one we admitted as Exhibit P1079.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was probably MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here in the middle, Karadzic says: "Okay. Tell me what's going on in Prijedor." Can you see this? This is a conversation between you and me on the 22nd of July, 1992; therefore, after the elections and after the government was formed seven months after the elections. Can you read this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic says: "Fine. Do you have any information ... they appointed a man in Prijedor last Friday afternoon. Now there is a Muslim commander and a Muslim mayor and Muslim chief of defence, Territorial Defence." Momcilo Mandic says: "I don't know. I'll look into it."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Was that one of those problems, where not even seven months after the inter-party agreement was the agreement honoured, and a Muslim was appointed to all these three posts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this is not an isolated case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to point this out and remind the witness of the background. Do you believe that the Serbs in Prijedor had reason for concern, in view of the fact that the war had already started in Croatia, there were rumours about people arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't know how people felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could all this be qualified as deceit and cheating and unlawful?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no deceit. It was simply failure to honour an agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now get 1D01393. I see the witness's answer was not recorded, that it was not lawful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it was not unlawful, because if the person appointed met the legal requirements, it was not unlawful; it was just failure to honour an agreement between parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it was contrary to the customs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the share of various communities in the total population, the first man in a certain field was supposed to be from one community, the second from the second most numerous communities, et cetera. That was not observed. But it was not unlawful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now get 1D01393.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that this is 11 February -- 12 February 1991? That's a month after the creation of the coalition government. Can you read this: "In estimating the security situation ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read this. I can't see well enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I'll do it. This was sent to all the municipal boards of the SDS and all the local boards and activists of the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It goes: "In estimating the security situation, we would like to point out two aspects that need to be clarified. First, the flats and houses of JNA Army members are marked with a special sign. And, second, rumours are going around about the -- about unlawful acquisition of weapons and --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Should it be of assistance, this is the Prosecution's 65 ter 01458. It's also D00259. And there is a translation available, if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which means that has been already admitted. Let's try that number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D259, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just to refresh your memory, this letter says that the homes of members of the JNA were being marked, just like in Croatia; and, second, there were rumours about people arming themselves. And now these boards are required to compile reports, with one copy to be sent to the party and another copy to the nearest army garrison. Do you see that, at this time, tensions were already being created through these rumours and also by marking the homes of JNA Army officers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this sort of thing happened in the Republic of Croatia and in the border-belt between Croatia and Bosnia, along the Una River. I don't know that it happened in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is already in evidence, I'd like to call 65 ter 30088. It's related to this topic. 30088.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, Witness, that Mr. Izetbegovic, all the way up to end January 1991, was in favour in preserving Yugoslavia, such as it was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because I provided security at those famous meetings between all the presidents of all Yugoslav republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the end of January, the SDA announced the adoption of the Declaration on Sovereignty, which was a step towards the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These tensions and all these rumours circulating in mid-February, do they indicate that it was precisely this announcement of independence that created these tensions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all I know, the Serbs wanted to stay within the old Yugoslavia, and Muslims did so for a while as well, and the first president of this rump Yugoslavia, without Slovenia, was to be a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I noted that the transcript says, at 96/18, "January 1991." I'm not sure that's what the question intended by way of the date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance: "Up to the end of January, 1991," that's what I asked the witness, "is it the case that the SDA and Izetbegovic were in favour of keeping the old Yugoslavia?" And the answer was: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was only at the end of January, the 31st of January, that the SDA announced the change in its policy, right after the elections?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the SDA changed its position in the end January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. You were not involved in politics, but the first attempt to endorse this document was in the end of January 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation between me and Zepinic, deputy minister, who was wire-tapped by his own service. Can we see the second page in both versions. Where it says "uh-huh."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Let me tell you, please, this reorganisation that's being carrying out, we have to see what this reorganisation will really mean, and also don't let them remove a single man of yours, if all of you don't want --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] " ... whether it's good or not. I have to sign something. Simovic sent me something to sign. Simovic does not inform me. It's somewhere with Doko. I told Simovic to call me urgently. He's at a Cabinet session. He was working --" Oh, I see here, it says where he was working. And now I wonder how it's possible that this young man will be moved from some service. Maybe we need him in that service. Maybe he's the only one we need there. But Simovic doesn't tell me about it. It's probably somewhere with Doko."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll stop here, page 4 in English. Do you remember that it was a frequent manipulation? A reorganisation was carried out to remove a Serb from a certain service where he could have an insight into what his colleagues were doing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on the police force, as I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about this Knezevic man who was in the Communication Service of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe during the war he was an assistant minister for communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that this Communication Service was also taken over by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that all this unlawful wire-tapping was not done by the MUP, but by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done by the service to which I also belonged, but there were people who took all these tapes, et cetera, to just one place, to the Party of Democratic Action, in other words. Of course, it was never the state, it was never the prosecutor, who ordered that someone should be wire-tapped in connection with some case or anything else. It was just party politics being pursued, routing for one party, and the leader of this entire team and the manager of this entire action was Munir Alibegovic, who in the 1980s had actually locked up Alija Izetbegovic in prison.
